intro: Most fast methods are not a bag of tricks. They reduce to a handful of ideas: place value, complements, the distributive law, factoring, doubling and halving, and remainders. These twelve skills carry most of the benefit; every guide in Track A is one of them in costume.

masters.title: Complements to 10, 100, 1,000
masters.rule: Know instantly what is missing to the next round number.

masters.title: Place-value decomposition
masters.rule: Split numbers by place and handle the big place first.

masters.title: Distributive property
masters.rule: a × (b + c) = ab + ac. Break a factor into easy pieces.

masters.title: Round and compensate
masters.rule: Use the nearby round number, then pay back the gap.

masters.title: Factor before calculating
masters.rule: Replace a multiplier or divisor with its factors; pair factors that make 10 or 100.

masters.title: Difference of squares
masters.rule: (a − b)(a + b) = a² − b². Name the center.

masters.title: Divisibility rules
masters.rule: Last digits, digit sums, and small trims tell you if a cut is clean.

masters.title: Memorize squares, powers, common fractions
masters.rule: Squares to 30, cubes to 10, powers of two, the fraction table.

masters.title: Estimate and independently check
masters.rule: Lock the magnitude first; check with digit roots or last digits.

progression.title: Difference of squares and square identities

notes.title: “Vedic Mathematics”
notes.body: The modern system called Vedic Mathematics comes from Bharati Krishna Tirtha’s 1965 book. Its arithmetic methods (vertical-and-crosswise, Nikhilam near-base, ends-in-5 squares) are legitimate. The claim that its 16 sutras come directly from ancient Vedic texts is historically disputed.

notes.title: “Japanese” line multiplication
notes.body: The viral line-drawing method has no well-established Japanese origin. Japan’s documented rapid-calculation tradition is the soroban and mental-abacus calculation (anzan).

notes.title: Chinese counting rods and the suanpan
notes.body: China calculated with counting rods on place-value boards, including multiplication, division, and square-root algorithms. The later suanpan bead abacus influenced Japan’s soroban.
